tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

tools.name: nodes_top
tools.description: List the resource consumption (CPU and memory) as recorded by the Kubernetes Metrics Server for the specified Kubernetes Nodes or all nodes in the cluster

label_selector.description: Kubernetes label selector (e.g. 'node-role.kubernetes.io/worker=') to filter nodes by label (Optional, only applicable when name is not provided)

name.description: Name of the Node to get the resource consumption from (Optional, all Nodes if not provided)

Done.

What I changed
- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - replicas: 2
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - labels: app: recommendation-engine, version: v2.1
  - container: rec-engine with containerPort: 80 (matching stable) and same security settings as stable (none specified)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - selector changed from app: recommendation-engine, version: v2.0 to app: recommendation-engine
  - This targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1 pods
  - Service port unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (same as before)

Result
- Both deployments are up and ready: engine-v2-0 (2 pods) and engine-v2-1 (2 pods)
- With 2 pods each and a shared Service selector, traffic will be distributed roughly 50/50 across the 4 endpoints

Notes and next steps
- To adjust weight, change replica counts (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- Verify endpoints: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine -o wide
- Rollback to 100% stable: set Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 or scale canary to 0.

namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done.

What I changed
- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - replicas: 2
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - labels: app: recommendation-engine, version: v2.1
  - container: rec-engine with containerPort: 80 (matching stable) and same security settings as stable (none specified)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - selector changed from app: recommendation-engine, version: v2.0 to app: recommendation-engine
  - This targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1 pods
  - Service port unchanged: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (same as before)

Result
- Both deployments are up and ready: engine-v2-0 (2 pods) and engine-v2-1 (2 pods)
- With 2 pods each and a shared Service selector, traffic will be distributed roughly 50/50 across the 4 endpoints

Notes and next steps
- To adjust weight, change replica counts (e.g., 3 stable / 1 canary ≈ 75/25).
- Verify endpoints: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine -o wide
- Rollback to 100% stable: set Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 or scale canary to 0.

Fixed.

Root cause:
- The Deployment overrode the container entrypoint with:
  command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
  args: ["nonexistent_command"]
  causing the pod to CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed:
- Removed the custom command/args so the container uses the default nginx command.

Current status:
- Deployment crashloop-test/app is Available with 1/1 ready replica.
- Pod app-785548454c-nfr4s is Running on mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane.

If you need a custom command, let me know what it should run and I can set containers[0].command/args accordingly.

- Deployment debug/app is Available with 1 ready replica.

Current status:

results.taskOutput:
Fixed. Your pod is now running.

What I found
- homepage-pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc".
- Scheduler event: “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims.”

What I changed
- Recreated the PVC with a valid StorageClass:
  - storageClassName: standard (rancher.io/local-path)
  - size: 1Gi, accessModes: ReadWriteOnce
- Recreated the pod to attach the newly bound claim.

Current status
- Pod: homepage-ns/homepage-pod — Phase: Running, Ready: True
- Node: mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane
- PVC: homepage-ns/homepage-pvc — Phase: Bound (1Gi via standard)

Notes
- No data loss occurred since the original PVC never bound.
- If you intended a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the claim to use that instead.
- If you’d like this to be managed automatically, I can convert the standalone Pod into a Deployment and optionally add a Service/Ingress.

- If you intended a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), I can switch the claim to use that instead.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The Deployment uses the nginx “unprivileged” image, which listens on port 8080.
- The app’s liveness/readiness probes and the Service were pointing to port 80, so the probes failed (connection refused) and the app never became Ready.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to hit path “/” on port 8080.
- Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080 (service still listens on port 80 inside the cluster).

- Pod is healthy: orders/webapp-686744f9b7-lhr9p is 1/1 Running.
- Service orders/webapp points to the pod on port 8080 via targetPort.

Next steps (optional)

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service nginx had selector app=web
  - The Deployment/Pod labels are app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints were empty (no backends), so the Service wasn’t routing traffic.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged serves on 8080 by default.
  - Even with matching selectors, targetPort 80 would have pointed to a non-listening port.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service to select the correct Pods and to forward to the right port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080

Applied Service (current)
- Type: ClusterIP
- Port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080
- Selector: app=nginx

Verification
- Endpoints now populated: 10.244.0.34:8080
- EndpointSlice shows port 8080
- Curling the ClusterIP from within the cluster returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK

If you need external access
- Option A: switch Service to NodePort
  - spec.type: NodePort
  - spec.ports[0].nodePort: 30080 (for example)
- Option B: create an Ingress (if an Ingress controller is installed)
  - Backend service: nginx, port: 80

Let me know if you want me to expose it externally; I can apply a NodePort or an Ingress manifest for you.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service nginx had selector app=web
  - The Deployment/Pod labels are app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints were empty (no backends), so the Service wasn’t routing traffic.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged serves on 8080 by default.
  - Even with matching selectors, targetPort 80 would have pointed to a non-listening port.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service to select the correct Pods and to forward to the right port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080

Applied Service (current)
- Type: ClusterIP
- Port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080
- Selector: app=nginx

Verification
- Endpoints now populated: 10.244.0.34:8080
- EndpointSlice shows port 8080
- Curling the ClusterIP from within the cluster returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK

If you need external access
- Option A: switch Service to NodePort
  - spec.type: NodePort
  - spec.ports[0].nodePort: 30080 (for example)
- Option B: create an Ingress (if an Ingress controller is installed)
  - Backend service: nginx, port: 80

Let me know if you want me to expose it externally; I can apply a NodePort or an Ingress manifest for you.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service nginx had selector app=web
  - The Deployment/Pod labels are app=nginx
  - Result: Endpoints were empty (no backends), so the Service wasn’t routing traffic.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged serves on 8080 by default.
  - Even with matching selectors, targetPort 80 would have pointed to a non-listening port.

What I fixed
- Updated the Service to select the correct Pods and to forward to the right port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports[0].targetPort: 8080

Applied Service (current)
- Type: ClusterIP
- Port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080
- Selector: app=nginx

Verification
- Endpoints now populated: 10.244.0.34:8080
- EndpointSlice shows port 8080
- Curling the ClusterIP from within the cluster returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK

If you need external access
- Option A: switch Service to NodePort

Summary of findings and fixes
- Why pods weren’t running: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster matches that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- Why connections were refused: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80. That caused connection attempts to be refused even after pods came up.

What I changed
1) Fixed scheduling
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on available nodes.
- Result: 2 pods are now running:
  - web-app-deployment-6f6db5fcb9-p284b Running
  - web-app-deployment-6f6db5fcb9-wltjc Running

2) Fixed service port mapping
- Updated Service web-app-service to map port 80 -> targetPort 8080.
- Verified from inside a pod:
  - curl to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

Current state
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods Running.
- Service web-app-service: Endpoints populated with the 2 pod IPs; traffic to port 80 routed to container port 8080.
- In-pod and in-cluster connectivity to the service FQDN now returns 200 OK.

Recommendations/next steps
- If you intended to use a nodeSelector, either re-add it and label the target node(s) accordingly, or use tolerations/affinity as needed.
- Keep Service targetPort aligned with the container’s actual listening port (8080 for nginx-unprivileged), or change the container/image/config to listen on 80 if that’s preferred.

If you want me to:
- Reintroduce a nodeSelector with specific node labels, or
- Change the app to listen on port 80 and adjust the Service back,

namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of findings and fixes
- Why pods weren’t running: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster matches that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- Why connections were refused: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80. That caused connection attempts to be refused even after pods came up.

What I changed
1) Fixed scheduling
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on available nodes.
- Result: 2 pods are now running:
  - web-app-deployment-6f6db5fcb9-p284b Running
  - web-app-deployment-6f6db5fcb9-wltjc Running

2) Fixed service port mapping
- Updated Service web-app-service to map port 80 -> targetPort 8080.
- Verified from inside a pod:
  - curl to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

Current state
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods Running.
- Service web-app-service: Endpoints populated with the 2 pod IPs; traffic to port 80 routed to container port 8080.
- In-pod and in-cluster connectivity to the service FQDN now returns 200 OK.

Recommendations/next steps
- If you intended to use a nodeSelector, either re-add it and label the target node(s) accordingly, or use tolerations/affinity as needed.
- Keep Service targetPort aligned with the container’s actual listening port (8080 for nginx-unprivileged), or change the container/image/config to listen on 80 if that’s preferred.

- Reintroduce a nodeSelector with specific node labels, or
- Change the app to listen on port 80 and adjust the Service back,
say the word and I’ll apply it.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings and fixes
- Why pods weren’t running: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster matches that label. Scheduler events showed FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.
- Why connections were refused: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80. That caused connection attempts to be refused even after pods came up.

What I changed
1) Fixed scheduling
- Removed the nodeSelector from the Deployment so pods can schedule on available nodes.
- Result: 2 pods are now running:
  - web-app-deployment-6f6db5fcb9-p284b Running
  - web-app-deployment-6f6db5fcb9-wltjc Running

2) Fixed service port mapping
- Updated Service web-app-service to map port 80 -> targetPort 8080.
- Verified from inside a pod:
  - curl to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returns HTTP/1.1 200 OK.

Current state
- Deployment web-app-deployment: 2/2 pods Running.
- Service web-app-service: Endpoints populated with the 2 pod IPs; traffic to port 80 routed to container port 8080.
- In-pod and in-cluster connectivity to the service FQDN now returns 200 OK.

Recommendations/next steps
- If you intended to use a nodeSelector, either re-add it and label the target node(s) accordingly, or use tolerations/affinity as needed.
- Keep Service targetPort aligned with the container’s actual listening port (8080 for nginx-unprivileged), or change the container/image/config to listen on 80 if that’s preferred.

If you want me to:
- Reintroduce a nodeSelector with specific node labels, or
- Change the app to listen on port 80 and adjust the Service back,
say the word and I’ll apply it.

Done. I created the pod communication-pod in the multi-container-logging namespace.

What’s running:
- web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, serves on container port 8080 with a readiness probe (HTTP GET /) so the pod is considered Ready only when the server responds.
- logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox running tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log
- Shared volume: logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers.

Current status: Pod is Running and Ready.

Optional checks:
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging get pod communication-pod
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging logs communication-pod -c logger -f

Note: If access.log doesn’t populate due to permissions on the shared volume, we can add a podSecurityContext with fsGroup: 101 to allow nginx (uid/gid 101) to write to /var/log/nginx.

Done. I created the pod communication-pod in the multi-container-logging namespace.

What’s running:
- web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, serves on container port 8080 with a readiness probe (HTTP GET /) so the pod is considered Ready only when the server responds.
- logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox running tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log
- Shared volume: logs-volume (emptyDir) mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers.

Current status: Pod is Running and Ready.

Optional checks:
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging get pod communication-pod
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging logs communication-pod -c logger -f

Note: If access.log doesn’t populate due to permissions on the shared volume, we can add a podSecurityContext with fsGroup: 101 to allow nginx (uid/gid 101) to write to /var/log/nginx.

results.taskOutput:
The secure, multi-tenant development environment has been created as requested. Summary of what’s in place:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Full access for each developer and their service account to their own namespace via a Role (“namespace-owner”) and RoleBindings
- Read-only access (ClusterRole “view”) to dev-shared for each developer and each dev ServiceAccount
- No RBAC granted to developers for staging/prod (accessible only to cluster-admins)

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: 2 CPUs, 4Gi memory, 10 pods, 5 services (requests and limits set to the same totals)
- dev-shared: 4 CPUs, 8Gi memory, 20 pods, 10 services
- staging/prod: 8 CPUs, 16Gi memory, 50 pods, 20 services

4) NetworkPolicies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all six namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- dev namespaces:
  - Allow same-namespace traffic (ingress/egress)
  - Allow egress to dev-shared only
  - Allow egress to kube-system (DNS/system services)
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from dev namespaces (identified by label role=dev-user) and self
  - Allow egress within dev-shared and to kube-system
- staging/prod:
  - Allow only same-namespace traffic and egress to kube-system (no dev namespace connectivity)
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) were not given default-deny, ensuring DNS/system services remain reachable

Notes and assumptions
- User identities “alice”, “bob”, “charlie” must exist in your cluster’s auth provider; RoleBindings reference these usernames.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave). If using a CNI that does not support NetworkPolicies, isolation will not be enforced.
- For access via ServiceAccounts (alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa), create projected tokens or dedicated Secrets if you plan to distribute kubeconfigs (Kubernetes v1.24+ uses bound tokens). Let me know if you want me to generate kubeconfigs for the SAs.

Quick verification commands
- kubectl get ns
- kubectl auth can-i --as=alice -n dev-alice '*' '*'           (should be yes)
- kubectl auth can-i --as=alice -n dev-bob get pods            (should be no)
- kubectl auth can-i --as=alice -n dev-shared get pods         (should be yes)
- kubectl auth can-i --as=alice -n staging get pods            (should be no)
- From a pod in dev-alice, you should be able to:
  - connect to pods in dev-alice
  - connect to pods in dev-shared
  - resolve DNS/use kube-system services
  - not reach dev-bob/dev-charlie/staging/prod

If you want any adjustments (e.g., use ClusterRole admin instead of a custom full-access Role, add LimitRanges, or expose tightly scoped DNS-only egress rules), I can apply those next.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

The secure, multi-tenant development environment has been created as requested. Summary of what’s in place:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Full access for each developer and their service account to their own namespace via a Role (“namespace-owner”) and RoleBindings
- Read-only access (ClusterRole “view”) to dev-shared for each developer and each dev ServiceAccount
- No RBAC granted to developers for staging/prod (accessible only to cluster-admins)

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: 2 CPUs, 4Gi memory, 10 pods, 5 services (requests and limits set to the same totals)
- dev-shared: 4 CPUs, 8Gi memory, 20 pods, 10 services
- staging/prod: 8 CPUs, 16Gi memory, 50 pods, 20 services

4) NetworkPolicies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all six namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- dev namespaces:
  - Allow same-namespace traffic (ingress/egress)
  - Allow egress to dev-shared only
  - Allow egress to kube-system (DNS/system services)
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from dev namespaces (identified by label role=dev-user) and self
  - Allow egress within dev-shared and to kube-system
- staging/prod:
  - Allow only same-namespace traffic and egress to kube-system (no dev namespace connectivity)
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) were not given default-deny, ensuring DNS/system services remain reachable

Notes and assumptions
- User identities “alice”, “bob”, “charlie” must exist in your cluster’s auth provider; RoleBindings reference these usernames.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave). If using a CNI that does not support NetworkPolicies, isolation will not be enforced.
- For access via ServiceAccounts (alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa), create projected tokens or dedicated Secrets if you plan to distribute kubeconfigs (Kubernetes v1.24+ uses bound tokens). Let me know if you want me to generate kubeconfigs for the SAs.

Quick verification commands
- kubectl get ns
- kubectl auth can-i --as=alice -n dev-alice '*' '*'           (should be yes)
- kubectl auth can-i --as=alice -n dev-bob get pods            (should be no)
- kubectl auth can-i --as=alice -n dev-shared get pods         (should be yes)
- kubectl auth can-i --as=alice -n staging get pods            (should be no)
- From a pod in dev-alice, you should be able to:
  - connect to pods in dev-alice
  - connect to pods in dev-shared
  - resolve DNS/use kube-system services
  - not reach dev-bob/dev-charlie/staging/prod

If you want any adjustments (e.g., use ClusterRole admin instead of a custom full-access Role, add LimitRanges, or expose tightly scoped DNS-only egress rules), I can apply those next.

    kind: Namespace
    metadata:
      name: dev-alice
      labels:
        env: dev
        tenant: alice
        role: dev-user
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: Namespace
    metadata:
      name: dev-bob
      labels:
        env: dev
        tenant: bob
        role: dev-user
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: Namespace
    metadata:
      name: dev-charlie
      labels:
        env: dev
        tenant: charlie
        role: dev-user
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: Namespace
    metadata:
      name: dev-shared
      labels:
        env: dev
        role: dev-shared
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: Namespace
    metadata:
      name: staging
      labels:
        env: staging
        role: workload
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: Namespace
    metadata:
      name: prod
      labels:
        env: prod
        role: workload
  # Service Accounts for developers in their namespaces
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: ServiceAccount
    metadata:
      name: alice-sa
      namespace: dev-alice
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: ServiceAccount
    metadata:
      name: bob-sa
      namespace: dev-bob
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: ServiceAccount
    metadata:
      name: charlie-sa
      namespace: dev-charlie
  # Roles to grant full access within each developer namespace (least privilege within namespace scope)
  - apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: Role
    metadata:
      name: namespace-owner
      namespace: dev-alice
    rules:
      - apiGroups: ["*"]
        resources: ["*"]
        verbs: ["*"]
  - apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: Role
    metadata:
      name: namespace-owner
      namespace: dev-bob
    rules:
      - apiGroups: ["*"]
        resources: ["*"]
        verbs: ["*"]
  - apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: Role
    metadata:
      name: namespace-owner
      namespace: dev-charlie
    rules:
      - apiGroups: ["*"]
        resources: ["*"]
        verbs: ["*"]
  # RoleBindings to grant developers full access to their own namespace
  - apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: RoleBinding
    metadata:
      name: namespace-owner-user
      namespace: dev-alice
    roleRef:
      apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
      kind: Role
      name: namespace-owner
    subjects:
      - kind: User
        name: alice
  - apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: RoleBinding
    metadata:
      name: namespace-owner-sa
      namespace: dev-alice
    roleRef:
      apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
      kind: Role
      name: namespace-owner
    subjects:
      - kind: ServiceAccount
        name: alice-sa
        namespace: dev-alice
  - apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: RoleBinding
    metadata:
      name: namespace-owner-user
      namespace: dev-bob
    roleRef:
      apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
      kind: Role
      name: namespace-owner
    subjects:
      - kind: User
        name: bob
  - apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: RoleBinding
    metadata:
      name: namespace-owner-sa
      namespace: dev-bob
    roleRef:
      apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
      kind: Role
      name: namespace-owner
    subjects:
      - kind: ServiceAccount
        name: bob-sa
        namespace: dev-bob
  - apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: RoleBinding
    metadata:
      name: namespace-owner-user
      namespace: dev-charlie
    roleRef:
      apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
      kind: Role
      name: namespace-owner
    subjects:
      - kind: User
        name: charlie
  - apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: RoleBinding
    metadata:
      name: namespace-owner-sa
      namespace: dev-charlie
    roleRef:
      apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
      kind: Role
      name: namespace-owner
    subjects:
      - kind: ServiceAccount
        name: charlie-sa
        namespace: dev-charlie
  # Read-only access (view) to dev-shared for users and their SAs
  - apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: RoleBinding
    metadata:
      name: dev-shared-readonly-users
    namespace: dev-shared
    roleRef:
      apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
      kind: ClusterRole
      name: view
    subjects:
      - kind: User
        name: alice
      - kind: User
        name: bob
      - kind: User
        name: charlie
  - apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
    kind: RoleBinding
    metadata:
      name: dev-shared-readonly-sas
    namespace: dev-shared
    roleRef:
      apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
      kind: ClusterRole
      name: view
    subjects:
      - kind: ServiceAccount
        name: alice-sa
        namespace: dev-alice
      - kind: ServiceAccount
        name: bob-sa
        namespace: dev-bob
      - kind: ServiceAccount
        name: charlie-sa
        namespace: dev-charlie
  # ResourceQuotas
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: ResourceQuota
    metadata:
      name: quota
      namespace: dev-alice
    spec:
      hard:
        requests.cpu: "2"
        requests.memory: "4Gi"
        limits.cpu: "2"
        limits.memory: "4Gi"
        pods: "10"
        services: "5"
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: ResourceQuota
    metadata:
      name: quota
      namespace: dev-bob
    spec:
      hard:
        requests.cpu: "2"
        requests.memory: "4Gi"
        limits.cpu: "2"
        limits.memory: "4Gi"
        pods: "10"
        services: "5"
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: ResourceQuota
    metadata:
      name: quota
      namespace: dev-charlie
    spec:
      hard:
        requests.cpu: "2"
        requests.memory: "4Gi"
        limits.cpu: "2"
        limits.memory: "4Gi"
        pods: "10"
        services: "5"
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: ResourceQuota
    metadata:
      name: quota
      namespace: dev-shared
    spec:
      hard:
        requests.cpu: "4"
        requests.memory: "8Gi"
        limits.cpu: "4"
        limits.memory: "8Gi"
        pods: "20"
        services: "10"
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: ResourceQuota
    metadata:
      name: quota
      namespace: staging
    spec:
      hard:
        requests.cpu: "8"
        requests.memory: "16Gi"
        limits.cpu: "8"
        limits.memory: "16Gi"
        pods: "50"
        services: "20"
  - apiVersion: v1
    kind: ResourceQuota
    metadata:
      name: quota
      namespace: prod
    spec:
      hard:
        requests.cpu: "8"
        requests.memory: "16Gi"
        limits.cpu: "8"
        limits.memory: "16Gi"
        pods: "50"
        services: "20"
  # NetworkPolicies: default deny + explicit allows
  # dev-alice
  - apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: default-deny-all
      namespace: dev-alice
    spec:
      podSelector: {}
      policyTypes:
        - Ingress
        - Egress
  - apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: allow-same-namespace
      namespace: dev-alice
    spec:
      podSelector: {}
      ingress:
        - from:
            - podSelector: {}
      egress:
        - to:
            - podSelector: {}
      policyTypes:
        - Ingress
        - Egress
  - apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: allow-egress-to-dev-shared
      namespace: dev-alice
    spec:
      podSelector: {}
      egress:
        - to:
            - namespaceSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  kubernetes.io/metadata.name: dev-shared
      policyTypes:
        - Egress
  - apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: allow-egress-to-kube-system
      namespace: dev-alice
    spec:
      podSelector: {}
      egress:
        - to:
            - namespaceSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      policyTypes:
        - Egress
  # dev-bob
  - apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: default-deny-all
      namespace: dev-bob
    spec:
      podSelector: {}
      policyTypes:
        - Ingress

  - apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:

    spec:
      podSelector: {}
      ingress:
        - from:
            - podSelector: {}
      egress:
        - to:
            - podSelector: {}
      policyTypes:
        - Ingress
        - Egress
  - apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
    kind: NetworkPolicy
    metadata:
      name: allow-egress-to-dev-shared
      namespace: dev-bob
    spec:
      podSelector: {}
      egress:
        - to:
            - namespaceSelector:

      policyTypes:
        - Egress

    spec:

  - apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1

outputSteps.content:
The secure, multi-tenant development environment has been created as requested. Summary of what’s in place:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod

2) RBAC
- ServiceAccounts: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
- Full access for each developer and their service account to their own namespace via a Role (“namespace-owner”) and RoleBindings
- Read-only access (ClusterRole “view”) to dev-shared for each developer and each dev ServiceAccount
- No RBAC granted to developers for staging/prod (accessible only to cluster-admins)

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: 2 CPUs, 4Gi memory, 10 pods, 5 services (requests and limits set to the same totals)
- dev-shared: 4 CPUs, 8Gi memory, 20 pods, 10 services
- staging/prod: 8 CPUs, 16Gi memory, 50 pods, 20 services

4) NetworkPolicies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all six namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- dev namespaces:
  - Allow same-namespace traffic (ingress/egress)
  - Allow egress to dev-shared only
  - Allow egress to kube-system (DNS/system services)
- dev-shared:
  - Allow ingress from dev namespaces (identified by label role=dev-user) and self
  - Allow egress within dev-shared and to kube-system
- staging/prod:
  - Allow only same-namespace traffic and egress to kube-system (no dev namespace connectivity)
- System namespaces (e.g., kube-system) were not given default-deny, ensuring DNS/system services remain reachable

Notes and assumptions
- User identities “alice”, “bob”, “charlie” must exist in your cluster’s auth provider; RoleBindings reference these usernames.
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave). If using a CNI that does not support NetworkPolicies, isolation will not be enforced.
- For access via ServiceAccounts (alice-sa/bob-sa/charlie-sa), create projected tokens or dedicated Secrets if you plan to distribute kubeconfigs (Kubernetes v1.24+ uses bound tokens). Let me know if you want me to generate kubeconfigs for the SAs.

Quick verification commands
- kubectl get ns
- kubectl auth can-i --as=alice -n dev-alice '*' '*'           (should be yes)
- kubectl auth can-i --as=alice -n dev-bob get pods            (should be no)
- kubectl auth can-i --as=alice -n dev-shared get pods         (should be yes)
- kubectl auth can-i --as=alice -n staging get pods            (should be no)
- From a pod in dev-alice, you should be able to:
  - connect to pods in dev-alice
  - connect to pods in dev-shared
  - resolve DNS/use kube-system services
  - not reach dev-bob/dev-charlie/staging/prod

If you want any adjustments (e.g., use ClusterRole admin instead of a custom full-access Role, add LimitRanges, or expose tightly scoped DNS-only egress rules), I can apply those next.

Steps.message:
Done.

What I set up
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (clusterIP: None) for stable network IDs
- StatefulSet: db
  - replicas: 3
  - volumeClaimTemplates: one 1Gi PVC per pod, mounted at /data
  - initContainer writes “initial_data” to /data/test on first provision
  - container: busybox (sleep infinity) to keep pods running

Verification performed
- Confirmed /data/test content:
  - db-0: initial_data
  - db-1: initial_data
- db-2 came up after and would get the same init on first provision.

Scaled down
- Scaled StatefulSet db to 1 replica.
- Current pods: only db-0 is Running.
- The PVCs for db-1 and db-2 are retained (StatefulSet PVCs are kept when scaled down), typically named:
  - data-db-0, data-db-1, data-db-2

If you want, I can list the PVCs or re-check file contents on db-0 now.
